summary.text: Early Earth, also called Proto-Earth, is loosely defined as the planet's first billion years, from its formation about 4.55 billion years ago to roughly 3.5 billion years ago.
In that time Earth built up from the solar nebula by accretion, and its air changed from mostly hydrogen and helium to a mix rich in nitrogen, methane and CO₂.
As the surface cooled and a crust formed, water vapor condensed into a superocean covering nearly the whole planet, turning a lava world into an ocean world where life soon appeared.

items.prompt: Earth's very first atmosphere was gathered from the same disk of gas that surrounded the young Sun. What was it mostly made of?
items.explain: The primary atmosphere, collected from the protoplanetary disk, was mostly hydrogen and helium; nitrogen, methane and CO₂ came later.

items.prompt: Earth started out as a lava planet but became an ocean planet. What mainly made the oceans appear?

options.label: The Moon's tides pulling water in
Cooling let water vapor rain out

items.explain: Once the surface cooled and formed a crust, most water vapor condensed out of the air into a superocean.

items.prompt: Proto-Earth was struck by another young planet, Theia. Roughly how big was Theia?
items.explain: Theia is described as a Mars-sized planet that shared Earth's orbit.

items.prompt: Proto-Earth was still sweeping up material from its neighborhood when the Moon-forming collision happened. How massive was it then, compared with Earth today?
items.explain: Proto-Earth was a protoplanet of about 0.63 Earth masses, still growing as it cleared its neighborhood.

items.prompt: What did the Moon-forming collision with Theia do to the young Earth?
items.explain: The collision led to a series of magma oceans and episodes of core formation.

items.prompt: After Earth's core formed, one idea says a late "veneer" brought it water and other volatile compounds. What would have carried them?
items.explain: Meteorites or comets from the outer Solar System might have delivered water to the mantle, crust and atmosphere in an intense bombardment.

pack.title: From Lava World to Ocean
pack.question: How did Earth change during its first billion years?

beats.title: From Lava World to Ocean
beats.hook: Earth began wrapped in hydrogen and helium, was melted by a planet-sized collision, and ended up as an ocean world with life.

beats.prompt: Put these stages of early Earth in order.

items.label: Earth builds up from the solar nebula by accretion
A collision with Theia leaves magma oceans
The crust cools and water vapor condenses into a superocean
The earliest known life forms appear

beats.explain: Earth first formed by accretion, was melted by the Moon-forming impact, then cooled enough for an ocean to form, and life appeared soon afterwards.

beats.prompt: A Mars-sized planet slams into the young Proto-Earth. What happens to Earth right afterwards?
beats.explain: The Moon-forming collision with Theia caused a series of magma oceans and episodes of core formation.

choices.label: Its rock melts into magma oceans
Nothing much changes
choices.feedback: A collision with a planet-sized body is far too big to leave Earth unchanged; it reshaped the planet.

choices.label: It freezes under clouds of dust
choices.feedback: Tempting if you picture an impact winter, but this collision delivered heat and melted rock.

beats.prompt: Sort each gas into the atmosphere it was mainly part of.
beats.explain: The first atmosphere came from the gas disk and was mostly hydrogen and helium; it was replaced by a secondary one rich in nitrogen, methane and CO₂.

beats.prompt: Match each name to what it is.

right.label: Bombardment that may have brought water
Oldest dated rock, about 4.404 billion years
Early crustal terrain about 3.8 billion years old

beats.explain: Each is a clue to early Earth: the impactor that made the Moon, the oldest dated mineral, some of the earliest surface terrains, and a possible source of water.

beats.idea: Earth grew by accretion, was melted into magma oceans by a giant impact, then cooled until its water vapor fell into a planet-wide ocean where life appeared.
